nameStory: The red-shouldered pine borer gets its name from the distinctive reddish-orange patches on its shoulder area, called the pronotum, which sits right behind its head. As a longhorn beetle whose larvae tunnel through pine wood, it truly earns the 'borer' part of its name by spending its youth creating winding galleries inside dead or dying pine trees.
description: The red-shouldered pine borer is a medium-sized longhorn beetle that's part of the diverse Cerambycidae family, known for their impressively long antennae. These beetles typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a sleek, somewhat flattened body. Their most striking feature is the bright reddish-orange coloring on their pronotum (the shield-like section behind the head), which contrasts beautifully with their darker wing covers. Like all longhorn beetles, they sport antennae that can be as long as or longer than their entire body.

idTips.label: Red shoulder patches
idTips.description: Look for bright reddish-orange coloring on the pronotum, the shield-like section right behind the head - this distinctive feature gives the beetle its common name

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: The antennae are nearly as long as the body or longer, typical of longhorn beetles, and feel slightly rough to the touch if you can observe one closely

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: The body is elongated and somewhat flattened, with a sleek appearance that feels smooth and hard when touched

idTips.label: Wing cover color
idTips.description: The elytra (wing covers) are typically dark brown to black, creating a strong contrast with the bright red shoulders

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Adults measure roughly 12-20mm long, about the size of your pinky nail to the first joint of your thumb

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Often found crawling on or flying around dead pine logs and stumps, moving with the deliberate pace typical of wood-boring beetles

habitat: Look for red-shouldered pine borers in coniferous forests throughout New England, particularly where white pine, red pine, and other pine species grow. They're most commonly found around recently dead or dying pine trees, fallen logs, and wood piles, since their larvae develop inside pine wood. You might spot adults on sunny days crawling across the bark of dead pines or visiting flowers near pine stands.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their wood galleries in late spring as temperatures warm. This is when you're most likely to spot them crawling on pine bark or flying between trees on warm, sunny days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, often found on flowers feeding on nectar or pollen. Mating occurs during this time, and females seek out suitable dead pine wood for egg-laying.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases as cooler weather arrives. Newly hatched larvae are busy boring into pine wood, though this happens invisibly inside the tree.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active, and larvae continue developing slowly inside their wood galleries. Look for old emergence holes in dead pine bark as evidence of past activity.

funFact: Despite being called a 'pine borer,' the larvae actually help forests by recycling dead wood back into soil nutrients - they're nature's cleanup crew, breaking down fallen trees that would otherwise pile up and create fire hazards!
confusionNotes: Red-shouldered pine borers can be confused with other longhorn beetles, but that distinctive red 'shoulder patch' on the pronotum is your best clue. Remember: 'Red shoulders, pine borer' - if you see bright reddish-orange coloring right behind the head on a longhorn beetle near pine trees, you've likely found your species.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'canadensis' means 'from Canada,' reflecting this beetle's wide distribution across northern North America. While the common name emphasizes pine as a host, these beetles can actually develop in various conifers, making them important decomposers in New England's mixed forests.
compareHints: Since this is the only Stictoleptura species in our dataset for New England, compare it with other longhorn beetles in the region. Most other longhorns lack the distinctive bright red shoulder patches that make this species so recognizable. The combination of red pronotum, dark wing covers, and association with pine wood creates a unique identification profile among New England's longhorn beetle community.
